doc.title: Larry Gold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2025

title: String section size, speakers and Sigma studio
summary: Gold's typical section, doubling against union rules, recording without headphones in the 1960s, and Phil Ramone's surprise at small Sigma.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: What's your preferred string section? If you have a decent budget do you like — how many violins violas, etcetera?

Well it all depends. In the old days I had six violins, two violas, and two cellos, which I still do a lot today. And much against union rules, I double that. And even back in the '70s and the '60s I used to double that. So, and that to me, if I get a couple of great performances that's plenty.
Did your string players, when you were overdubbing and doubling did they like to hear what they just played in their headphones?
Sometimes yes, some of them would, and sometimes no.

You know when I first started playing on records we didn't even have earphones. We used little speakers. There was a speaker in the room and everybody just could hear each other. And then I guess when we doubled it they reversed the phase on or something © Fillius Jazz Archive 4

somehow they canceled out the speaker. And the speaker couldn't be really loud so there was usually one speaker in front of the cellos and violas and maybe one speaker to the side of the violins, and maybe one to the other side. And that was the way, all through the '60s that's how we did it in Philadelphia.
It must have contributed, even marginally to the sound of those records because you're recording the room on the overdub even though you might have been trying to avoid it, you're still getting that.

I think you're right, you know I think you're right. You know Phil Ramone came down late '70s one time to record something. And I was playing that time, and I even think I helped him get the section together. And he said, he couldn't believe how small Sigma was. The ceilings weren't very high. The room dimension was really small. He was used to big rooms you know. I mean but he was amazed that Joe Tarsia got that great sound from such a small room.
